How can we possibly afford a universal basic income? This appears to be the strongest argument against an income scheme. It also illustrates one of the basic problems in economic analysis. When macroeconomic professors stand at the black board they generally draw an x-shaped graph and label one line to represent the real or physical part the economy and the other to represent the financial side. This is an important distinction because if one analyses economic problems only in financial terms the complexities of the financial system get in the way of clearly seeing problems.  Too often economic problems are analyzed in financial terms. In the case of the universal basic income the question should be are we capable of producing enough goods and services to provide everyone with the desired standard of living.  The answer should determine the level of the basic income. There are a number of economic issues with which we need to deal:  we have extracted the most easily accessible energy and mineral resources and those left require a lot of energy to get; there are serious problems resulting from the fractional reserve way of creating money; the work ethic is a problem in a high technology world; and there is a need to recognize our economy, what we call capitalism,  is based on legislation which restricts competition and allows some people to make profits they would otherwise not get. I believe most of these need to dealt with at the same time.  Certainly a UBI should be introduced at the same time as a reform of the financial system. These are complex emotional issues and will be extremely difficult to resolve. The book Funny Money: Adapting to a Down Economy, by the author of this post discusses these issues. Please have a look at it.

Basic income has absolutely nothing to do with socialism. Socialism is in the classical sense the idea of government controlling important industries with the proceeds from those industries split among the people. Rather than rehash the debate myself, here is a libertarian perspective endorsement of basic income from Cato. Another one also as part of a discussion with the Cato Institute. Hayek also supported a basic income guarantee.

One thing those articles do not directly touch on is one that I think is most important - productivity. One of the most fundamentally critical ratios in the free market is the number of people required to produce the goods and services for for a certain population of people. Basically a very macro scale measure of overall productivity. Across the world this ratio is decreasing. In America in the 50s if it took 50 people to produce the goods and services for 100 people, those same workers can now produce the goods and services for 250 people. Cross sector productivity has increased to 250%. Put another way we've gone from requiring a hypothetical 50 people to produce the goods and services for 100 people to just 20 people.

As the ratio continues to shrink, things like a basic income will become mandatory. It's not like reducing the population changes the problem. It's an issue of ratios that exists with 1 billion people, 100 million, or even just 100,000. The reason you see so many libertarian minded Silicon Valley types advocating for a basic income is this very phenomena. They understand where automation is taking us and as those articles also hit, we will reach a point where a basic income is not a luxury but simple a matter of sustaining a functional society.
